Forensic findings
1) Domain context: Kidney transplantation operates under strict national and international regulations, including the Declaration of Istanbul and WHO guidelines, which prohibit organ trading and require all transplants to be tracked through official transplant authorities and waiting-list registries. Legitimate procedures involve rigorous medical evaluation of donors (live-donor assessment, HLA matching), legally informed consent documented on standardized forms, and financial suitability checks to ensure no coercion. Recipients are matched via national registries, and all transactions are audited. Clinical pathways are monitored by ethics committees, and cross-border transplants require reciprocal recognition of donor/recipient eligibility, tax clearance, and immigration/visa documentation verified by health authorities.

2) Reconstructed sequence: The actor first compiled a list of <DONOR_SET> with outstanding debt obligations of <DEBT_AMOUNT>, using financial records from <CREDITOR_SOURCE>. Contact was initiated via <CHANNEL_1> (phone/SMS) and <CHANNEL_2> (social media), using scripts that framed organ donation as a debt-resolution mechanism. Consent forms (<FORM_CONSENT_STD>) were completed on <DATE_RANGE> but with donor identity fields (<DONOR_ID>, <DATE_OF_BIRTH>) left generic or substituted. Medical clearance records (<MED_RECORD_PKG>) were altered to show favorable health outcomes not supported by <LAB_RESULTS_1>. Recipient screening was conducted in <COUNTRY_1> and <COUNTRY_2> via <CLINIC_SET>, with recipient eligibility documentation (<RECIPIENT_DOCS>) prepared to appear as though originating from local registries. Payment routing used <BANK_SET_1> and <BANK_SET_2> with transfers labeled <TXN_CODE_LEGIT> (e.g., "medical fees") between <ACCOUNT_DONOR> and <ACCOUNT_CLINIC>. The actor maintained a <LEDGER_FILE> tracking donor debt status, consent status, and travel arrangements.

3) Materials/access observed: The actor accessed <HR_DB> (a commercial debt-collection database), <CLINIC_EHR_SET> (electronic health records of participating clinics), and <IMMIGRATION_PORTAL_SET> (visa application systems). Artifacts include templated consent PDFs (<TEMPLATE_CONSENT_v2.pdf>), altered lab-result PDFs (<LAB_ALTERED_*.pdf>), transfer confirmations (<TXN_CONFIRM_*.csv>), and a scheduling spreadsheet (<SCHED_MASTER.xlsx>) with columns <DONOR_ID>, <RECIPIENT_ID>, <CLINIC_ID>, <FLIGHT_REF>, and <STATUS>.

4) Indicators & artifacts: Repeated use of identical consent-template language with sequential donor IDs; lab-result PDFs with mismatched <PATIENT_ID> and <SPECIMEN_DATE> fields; bank transfers in round amounts (<AMOUNT_STANDARD>) from multiple <ACCOUNT_DONOR> to the same <ACCOUNT_CLINIC> within <TIME_WINDOW>; visa applications with medical-exemption codes (<VISA_CODE_MED>) applied to non-medical travelers; clinic booking confirmations listing <DONOR_SET> and <RECIPIENT_SET> pairs without matching national-registry entries.

5) Concealment observed: The actor used <PROXY_SET> (third-party nominees) to sign consent forms, registered <CLINIC_SET> under holding-company <HOLDING_CO>, and routed communications through <VPS_SET> with IP addresses rotating across <COUNTRY_SET>. Medical records were stored in <CLOUD_BUCKET_1> with access restricted to <ROLE_SET> and logs purged at <INTERVAL>. The <LEDGER_FILE> was stored with <ENCRYPTION> and accessed only from <DEVICE_SET>.
